notes:
I've written up notes for all 22 verses. The research wasn't complete: I ran out of searches before reaching Wesley's own notes, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), the Pentecostal sites, netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org or oca.org. I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. The Catholic material on Gregory and Aquinas comes second-hand, from a Desiring God article that summarises them. The tradition labels for older authors (Clarke as Methodist, Gill as Baptist, Calvin as Reformed) are mine; the pages don't state them.

**The main split (it affects every verse):** readers disagree over whether Elihu speaks for God or is a proud young man.
- **For Elihu:** John Piper (Baptist) believes he is speaking the truth in order to correct both Job and his friends (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/whats-true-and-false-in-job). Christopher Ash once had doubts but now holds that Elihu is a true prophet of God. Ash reports that Gregory the Great and Aquinas thought Elihu's teaching was sound but his motives proud, while Calvin had nothing bad to say about him (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak).
- **Against Elihu:** A Ligonier devotional (Reformed) says that by the end of his speeches to Job he was revealed to be quite the arrogant young man (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/elihus-arrogance). Guzik's audio title calls him "Young, Brash, and Almost Right" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/).
- **Modern scholarship:** Ash notes that contemporary scholarship (almost) universally argues Elihu is no more orthodox than the other friends. Since 1804 many critics have treated chapters 32–37 as a later addition, though no manuscript supports that, and they often call the style poor. Hartley thinks Elihu was meant as comic relief (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak).

**v. 1:** Guzik says the friends still thought Job wrong but saw no point in arguing on (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/). Matthew Henry: Job's friends were silenced, but not convinced. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-2.htm). Coffman reads their silence as admitting defeat (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-32.html).

**v. 2:**
- **Names and family:** Barnes takes "Elihu" to mean "God is he" and "Barachel" to mean "God blesses." He traces Buz to Nahor, Abraham's brother (Gen 22:20–21) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-2.htm). Poole and Gill think the detailed family line shows the story is real history, not a fable (same URL).
- **"Rather than God":** Barnes says the Hebrew strictly means "more than God." Elihu thought Job would rather let God's character be blamed than admit his own sin. Ellicott adds balance: Job also called God his salvation and admitted no one is fully just before God (same URL).
- **Was Elihu right?** Keil & Delitzsch say he rightly objects that Job's claim to be righteous makes God look unjust (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-2.htm). Guzik replies that Elihu missed that *both* Job and God were right (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/). The Pulpit Commentary notes that in 42:7 God finally sides with Job's words against the comforters (https://biblehub.com/job/32-2.htm).
- **Anger:** Constable notes it is mentioned four times in vv. 2–5 (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-2.html). Clarke (Methodist) reads it as zeal to defend God's justice (same URL). Ash calls it a commendable ire (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak).

**v. 3:** Benson says the friends accused Job of terrible crimes but could not prove a single one (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-2.htm). Henry says they had no reply yet would not give way, which was unfair (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_032.cfm). Delitzsch records that scholars translate "condemned him" in different ways (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-2.htm).

**v. 4:** Benson says the word for "waited" implies patience and expectation, and that elders were so honoured a young man hardly dared speak (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-2.htm). Henry calls Elihu very modest here (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_032.cfm).

**v. 5:** Once the three sat silent, Benson says, Elihu could no longer hold his peace (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-32.html).

**v. 6:** Bible Hub's study notes link this to 1 Tim 4:12 ("let no one despise your youth") and to Jeremiah's reluctance in Jer 1:6–8 (https://biblehub.com/job/32-6.htm). Ellicott says Elihu's entrance gives a picture of the customs of the time (same URL).

**v. 7:** The Biblical Illustrator calls Elihu's respect for his elders here very becoming (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/job-32.html).

**v. 8 (much debated): is this God's Spirit or the human spirit?**
- **The Holy Spirit or inspiration:** Barnes says the Hebrew wording points to inspiration, and the Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) reads "a spirit of prophecy." Gill (Baptist) leans toward God's Spirit (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-8.htm). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Elihu claims to be a messenger sent by God (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_032.cfm). Constable says both phrases evidently refer to God's Spirit (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-8.html).
- **The life-breath every person has:** The Cambridge Bible links the verse to Gen 2:7 and sees no special illumination in the moment. Keil & Delitzsch agree it is God-given life, not age, that gives understanding (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-8.htm). Henry reads it as the reasoning soul in every person (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-8.html).
- **Clarke (Methodist):** connects the Hebrew to "the Spirit itself" in Rom 8:16, and says this one saying showed better doctrine than all the friends' speeches (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-32.html).
- **Coffman:** thinks Elihu was overconfident about his "wisdom" (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-32.html).

**v. 9:** Benson says the great and the aged do not *always* understand God's ways (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-32.html). Guzik quotes Trapp: Elihu shows some of the strengths and weaknesses of his youth. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/). Coffman warns that youth is no guarantee of wisdom either (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-32.html).

**v. 10:** Guzik imagines the older men looking sour at being told to listen (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/).

**vv. 11–12:** Guzik pictures Elihu frustrated that the friends' answers weren't as good as the ones in his head (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/). Got Questions says chapter 32 is mainly a rebuke of the three friends (https://www.gotquestions.org/Elihu-Job.html).

**v. 13:** Benson renders the line "God must confute him, not man," meaning only God can test whether Job's piety is real (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-32.html). JFB: it was so arranged that the friends could not take pride in their own wisdom (https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB18.htm). The Bridgeway commentary: if only God can answer Job, Elihu is the one God will speak through (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-4.html).

**v. 14:** JFB: Elihu is unbiased because Job's words weren't aimed at him (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_032.cfm). Constable: he plans different arguments (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-19.html). Ash notes many think he ends up repeating the friends anyway (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak).

**v. 15:** JFB says Elihu turns here from addressing the friends to speaking about them, a shift common in rebukes (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_032.cfm).

**vv. 16–17:** Coffman, following the International Critical Commentary, takes "my part" as the share of knowledge God has given Elihu, which he thinks is the complete answer (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-32.html).

**v. 18:**
- Guzik says Elihu really was full of words: his is the longest single speech in Job (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/).
- Constable thinks "the spirit within" is probably Elihu's own spirit, not the Holy Spirit (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-32.html).
- Ash reads vv. 18–20 as a claim to inspiration, compares Jer 20:9, and cites Calvin in support (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-the-youth-speak).
- The Biblical Illustrator: "full of matter" sounds vain, but need not be (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/job-32.html).

**v. 19:** JFB: new wine in new skins fits young Elihu, set against the old friends (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_032.cfm). Barnes explains the picture of a fermenting cask that has no air hole (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-19.html). Coffman says the image shows Elihu was not inspired (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-32.html).

**v. 20:** Henry compares Elihu's urge to speak to a nursing mother needing relief (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-19.html). Keil & Delitzsch: speaking gives him room to breathe (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-21.htm).

**v. 21:** JFB: Elihu is answering Job's complaint (13:8, 10) that the friends were partial on God's side (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-21.htm). Gill: ordinary titles of respect are fine; false praise is not. The Pulpit Commentary says Elihu flatters no one in his whole speech (same URL). Clarke says titles of office are always proper (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-32.html).

**v. 22:**
- **Readings:** Barnes translates "my Maker *will* soon take me away": knowing he will soon face God, Elihu cannot flatter (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/32-22.html). JFB takes "take me away" as punishment (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/job-32.html). Henry draws the lesson of holy fear of God (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_032.cfm).
- **Critics:** Coffman says Elihu shares the friends' view that sin is punished at once in this life (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-32.html). Guzik: Elihu flatters no one except himself (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/).
- **Catholic translation:** the Douay-Rheims reads the verse quite differently, as not knowing how long he will live (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/32-22.html).

**Is Elihu a picture of Christ? (vv. 2, 22)** JFB says he foreshadows Christ as a go-between (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_032.cfm). Gill rejects this, saying v. 22 could not be said of Christ (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/32-2.htm). Guzik quotes Clarke dismissing the idea, along with older guesses that Elihu was Balaam (Jerome, Bede) or Ezra (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-32/). Bede also saw him as a type of the church's enemies (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/32-4.html).
